opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Arjun. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how people see changes at work, and nothing you tell me will be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, happy to. I install the robots, so I'm probably at the optimistic end of the people you talk to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and people should learn it. Same as I'd say about any new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This version's fine for me. I'd still be installing robot cells, and the AI just helps me write code and documents faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing installs. Take a course on the newer vision systems. Maybe pitch a side project at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit of 'is that all?'

S0.say: It's a useful tool, and people should learn it.
S0.think: Fine for me. I still install robot cells, and AI helps me write code faster.
S0.do: Keeps doing installs, takes a course on newer vision systems and pitches a side project.
S0.feel: Calm, a bit of 'is that all?'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow adoption gives everyone time to upskill. That's the good news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm fine. Fewer junior hires is a shame, but juniors can learn online now. That's how I see it, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mentor a couple of technicians at the plant. Keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said juniors can learn online. Is that enough to get hired when firms want fewer of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not for everyone. But it's what I'd tell them. Effort still counts.

S1.say: Slow adoption gives everyone time to upskill.
S1.think: I'm fine. Fewer junior hires is a shame, but juniors can learn online.
S1.do: Mentors a couple of plant technicians and keeps learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the new AI jobs are real, and people who lose office work should retrain into them. The government should fund that rather than pay people to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good for me. Every company wants automation now, and there aren't enough people who can install it and commission it, which means getting it running properly on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask for a raise, or move to a company that pays more. Maybe start consulting on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Busy.

S2.say: The new AI jobs are real. Fund retraining, not paying people to sit at home.
S2.think: Good for me. Everyone wants automation and there aren't enough people who can get it running.
S2.do: Asks for a raise or moves to a better-paying firm, and starts weekend consulting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same line. Retrain, adapt, and the market will create new jobs. Maybe with some help for people in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Here's what nags me. If AI matches skilled engineers at thinking work, a lot of my design and programming is done by the AI. What's left is being on the floor with my hands on the equipment. Still a job, but not the one I trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spend more time on the floor and less at the desk. Get really good at the hands-on side. Put some money from the share boom into robotics companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, which surprises me.

S3.say: Retrain and adapt. The market will create new jobs, with some help for people in between.
S3.think: AI could do most of my design and programming. What's left is hands-on floor work, not the job I trained for.
S3.do: Spends more time on the shop floor and puts some boom gains into robotics companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest opportunity in a generation for people who build robots. And everyone else can learn to work alongside them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, this is the best case. Every warehouse, farm and kitchen needs robots installed, tuned and fixed. That's me. I'd be in demand for a decade. I know it's rough for the people the robots replace, but they can retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start my own integration firm, probably. Hire a few technicians from the plant who want to learn. Charge a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Really excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they can retrain. Picture a 41-year-old line worker with two kids and no savings. How does that work for her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I don't know. Paid training, I'd say. But I can't really picture her doing my job. I guess I don't think about that part much.

S4.say: This is the biggest opportunity in a generation for people who build robots.
S4.think: Best case for me. I'd be in demand for a decade. It's rough for the people replaced, but they can retrain.
S4.do: Plans to start his own robot integration firm, hiring plant technicians who want to learn.
